name: Meal prep

lead: Meal prep means planning and cooking meals in advance, often a week at a time, and storing them in portions. Fitness communities use it to hit calorie and protein targets consistently, which supports fat loss or muscle gain and a better physique over time.

The chain is food ready to eat, fewer unplanned choices, and an easier time sticking to a diet. Small studies exist: one six-week group-based program reported better cooking attitudes, behaviours and body composition.

paras: People usually cook once or twice a week, portion proteins, carbs and vegetables into containers and keep them in the fridge or freezer. It is combined with any diet pattern, from bulking to cutting, and the benefit builds with consistency over weeks.

Stored cooked food can grow bacteria if kept or reheated improperly, so food-safety storage matters. Some plastic containers can shed microplastics when heated, which is why some people reheat in glass or ceramic.

chain: Steady fat loss or muscle gain
angle.text: Meal prep helps you hit calorie and protein targets every day, which drives steady fat loss or muscle gain and a better physique over time. Portioned meals cut decision-making and unplanned eating. Small studies link prep programs to better eating habits and body composition.

lead: Meal prep is the practice of planning and cooking meals in advance, often a week at a time, and storing them in portioned containers [1]. In fitness and appearance communities it is used to hit calorie and protein targets consistently, which is how many people lose body fat or build muscle: a diet that is easy to follow is one that gets followed, and having cooked portions ready reduces unplanned or convenience eating.

Wikipedia notes people use it to lose weight, build muscle or keep a healthy lifestyle, and links frequent home cooking with lower type 2 diabetes risk [1]. A small published pilot study reported that a six-week group-based advanced meal prep course improved cooking attitudes, behaviours and body composition [2].

Meal prep is a habit rather than a product, and its relevance to looks runs through diet adherence: portion control, steady protein for training, and fewer decisions at mealtimes. It is also associated with saving money compared with eating out [1].
infobox: Batch cooking, advance quantity meal prep
Portion and calorie control, protein intake, convenience, cost saving
Small labelled, dated containers (plastic or glass)

paras: Fully cooked meals are made ahead to standardise portions and are often stored in small labelled, dated containers [1]. Related services include meal kits and meal delivery companies.

The pilot program in the research literature had participants meet weekly in a commercial kitchen to prepare meals in bulk and package individual portions, taking home 10 meals and 5 snacks each week [2]. Meal prep sits alongside meal kits and delivery services as ways to shift cooking time and decisions earlier in the week.

Bodybuilding-style diets rely on repeatable meals: the same protein, carbohydrate and vegetable portions at set times. Users prepare them in batches so that fixed targets are hit without daily cooking. On looksmax.org, a member describing a diet of fasting and low-carbohydrate eating complained that broccoli and chicken breast were boring and asked for low-carb prep ideas [3], and another thread asked whether UK members used meal prep companies [4].

Wikipedia cites a restaurant menu markup of around 300 percent and US figures showing food-at-home spending rising 6.4 percent while food-away-from-home spending fell 32.6 percent between 2019 and 2020, estimating that the average consumer saved about $1,151 by eating out less [1].

Cohort analyses cited by Wikipedia link eating home-prepared meals more often with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes, and associate more ultra-processed food and eating out with higher risk of hypertension, dyslipidaemia or cancer; a systematic review found frequent eating out associated with higher sugar and fat intake and lower iron, calcium and vitamin C intake [1]. These studies concern home cooking in general rather than batch preparation specifically.

Pre-cooked food can grow bacteria if stored improperly or eaten too late, and plastic containers can shed microplastics, particularly when microwaved [1]. Wikipedia also notes that over-structured prepping can lead to rigidity or a food rut [1].
Wikipedia also notes that freezing can make plastic containers more brittle and that "microwave-safe" labelling describes structural integrity more than chemical safety [1].
Meal prep is discussed alongside bodybuilding-style diets and low-carbohydrate eating, with users asking about prep ideas and meal prep companies in forum threads [4][3].
Discussion tends to be practical: what to cook, which services to use, and how to make restricted diets tolerable. Meal prep is rarely the subject of claims; it is treated as logistics for a diet.

A pilot study in Current Developments in Nutrition tested a group-based advance quantity meal prep (AQMP) program in participants recruited from a fitness center, with one group measured before the program, right after it and three months later. The program met weekly for six weeks in a commercial kitchen. Cooking attitude scores rose from baseline to three months, cooking self-efficacy rose by the end of the program, and reported home-cooked dinners increased from about 52 percent to 86 percent. Mean body weight fell from 85.1 kg to 83.3 kg at three months, fat mass fell from 32.0 kg to 28.6 kg, and BMI fell from 31.7 to 31.0 at the end of the program. The authors describe it as a pilot and call for larger controlled studies [2][5].

A pilot of a community meal-kit service in Washington DC studied vegetable intake and barriers to healthy eating rather than appearance [6]. No trial has compared meal prep with other adherence strategies for body composition.
